what_it_does: When chip designers plan a new system-on-chip (SoC) — a single piece of silicon that houses a general-purpose processor plus specialized hardware accelerators for graphics, AI, and so on — they need to predict how well different combinations of components will perform before spending billions on manufacturing. Existing quick-estimation tools only considered two extreme scenarios: 'all programs run perfectly in parallel' or 'nothing runs in parallel at all.' Real workloads sit somewhere in between: several independent applications run at the same time, each with its own mix of phases that must execute in a particular order. HILP models this realistic middle ground by framing the scheduling of those multi-phase applications across the SoC's mixed set of cores and accelerators as a mathematical optimization problem (called integer linear programming, or ILP — a method that finds the best assignment among a huge number of choices by solving a set of logical constraints). The ILP solver finds a near-optimal schedule that minimizes total run time while respecting power and memory-bandwidth limits, enabling chip architects to sweep through thousands of design candidates quickly during early planning.
